extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of sociology/psychology/philosophy of humour; researchers studying theories and functions of laughter
extracted.subtask_description: Theoretical and sociological analysis of laughter and humour, focused on Bergson's account and its relation to earlier theories (incongruity, superiority, physiological accounts) and on the social functions humour performs. Useful for scholars constructing or evaluating theories of the comic and humour's social roles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reality of duration vs discrete mental states
rubrics_metrics.description: Experience cannot comprise a sequence of distinct states of mind; language and conventional psychology mislead by 'arresting and solidifying into finished things' that are in fact fluid (Bergson).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing humour or laughter, avoid models that treat mental states as discrete, instantaneous events. Instead account for the continuous flow of experience (duration) and how past themes and future expectations weave into present perception. Critique theories that rely on a single identifiable moment of change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suddenness/quickness in incongruity/superiority theories
rubrics_metrics.description: Classical theories (Locke, Hobbes, Schopenhauer, Campbell) assume that perception of incongruity or superiority must be sudden or 'quick' to produce wit or laughter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If using or evaluating incongruity/superiority accounts, note they typically require a sudden break or surprise; but these accounts rarely specify what constitutes sufficient suddenness. Be explicit about tempo/expectation breaches when arguing that suddenness causes laughter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Muscular activity constitutive of emotional intensity
rubrics_metrics.description: Following James and Bergson: the muscular reaction produces the feeling of intensity (we are sad because we weep; fear because we run); muscular involvement partly constitutes emotional experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyses of laughter should account for bodily/muscular components: loud, bodily laughter contributes to subjective intensity. Do not assume inner intensity automatically causes muscular display; consider the reverse causal or constitutive relation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laughter is human
rubrics_metrics.description: Laughter is principally directed at humans; we only laugh at animals or things insofar as they suggest human qualities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When identifying comic targets, prioritize human behaviour or human-like attributes. Objects or animals are comic only when they evoke human characteristics; this centers ridicule in human social relations rather than in the environment or inanimate nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Momentary absence of feeling (anaesthesia of the heart)
rubrics_metrics.description: Laughter involves a temporary suspension of usual social feelings (pity, affection): 'we must, for the moment, put our affection out of court and impose silence upon our pity.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat laughter as involving a momentary withholding of empathy; analyses should recognize the 'cruel' or depersonalizing dimension of laughter and examine contexts where sympathy is deliberately suspended.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laughter is socially shared (needs an echo)
rubrics_metrics.description: Laughter 'appears to stand in need of an echo' — it reverberates among people and is typically 'always the laughter of a group.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Methodologically, study laughter as a social phenomenon: observe group dynamics and how laughter spreads, rather than relying solely on individual introspection. Accounts should explain how social contagion, audience, and group membership shape laughter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize social function/utility (la fonction utile)
rubrics_metrics.description: Instead of asking 'What causes the individual to laugh?', Bergson urges asking 'What are the social effects of laughter?' and seeking laughter's social utility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame research questions in functional terms: what effects does humour have on social relations, order, control, or cohesion? Evaluate theories by their capacity to explain social consequences, not just individual cognitive triggers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessary vs surplus functions of humour
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish functions that are universal/necessary for social life from those that are surplus/specific to particular social arrangements (borrowing Spencer's biological-functional distinctions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When cataloguing humour's functions, classify whether a function is necessary for the continuity of social life or merely situational/surplus. Theorists should be explicit if they claim a function to be foundational (necessary) rather than context-specific.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic arises from rigidity/mechanical behaviour
rubrics_metrics.description: Bergson's core claim: laughter is provoked by rigid or mechanical behaviour — 'the attitudes, gestures and movements of the human body are laughable in exact proportion as that body reminds us of a mere machine' and the comic is 'something mechanical encrusted on the living.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify examples of inelasticity, rigidity, or mechanized behaviour in subjects of humour. Explain how the impression of a human acting like a thing (loss of flexibility, automatism) elicits ridicule rather than treating all incongruity as comic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations of incongruity and degradation theories
rubrics_metrics.description: Theories of incongruity or degradation cover only part of the comic; they fail to explain why some incongruities or misfortunes are comic and others tragic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid using incongruity or degradation as blanket explanations. Specify the particular subset of incongruities (e.g., mechanical rigidity producing misfortune) that generate laughter, and justify why other incongruities are non-comic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Joke-structures: finished, not sympathy-inviting
rubrics_metrics.description: Joke narratives are usually self-contained ('finished'); listeners do not ask what happens next and are not expected to express sympathy for joke-figures — pain/cruelty in jokes paves the way to punch-lines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing jokes, note their narrative closure and the social expectation that recipients respond with amusement rather than compassion. Use examples (ethnic jokes, blind-man joke) to illustrate how suffering is instrumental to punch-lines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fine's three social functions of humour
rubrics_metrics.description: Gary Fine proposed three particularly general functions: promoting group cohesion, provoking intergroup conflict, and providing social control.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these three analytic categories to evaluate humour in social contexts: does the humour solidify in-group bonds, mark or provoke conflict with out-groups, or operate to control behaviour and enforce norms?

rubrics_metrics.name: Attardo: decommitment and group identification
rubrics_metrics.description: Attardo identifies two broad social/interpersonal functions: 'decommitment' (allowing speakers to soften or mitigate socially risky statements) and 'group identification.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply Attardo's categories to interpret humorous moves that enable face-saving or boundary-marking. Check whether humour is used to distance speakers from a statement (decommitment) or to signal membership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conversational/interpersonal functions of humour
rubrics_metrics.description: Analysts (Graham et al., Hay, Holmes, Norrick, Janet Holmes) catalogue many conversational functions: expressing solidarity, meeting solidarity-based/power-based/psychological needs, face-saving, easing tension, testing common ground, creating rapport, metalingual labeling of inappropriate talk, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In micro-analytic studies of interaction, map specific humour uses to these conversational functions; recognize that humour often serves multiple interactional tasks simultaneously and that different contexts privilege different functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humour's positive and negative functions; critical stance
rubrics_metrics.description: Humour may serve both beneficial and harmful functions (solidarity vs provocation or ridicule). Many analysts show a bias emphasizing positives, but Bergson emphasizes humour's 'cold cruelty' even as it yields useful social effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critically evaluate both the sociopositive and socionegative effects of humour. Do not assume benefits outweigh harms; explicitly consider how humour can both maintain cohesion and produce exclusion, mockery, or dehumanization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method: observe others, not introspect
rubrics_metrics.description: Bergson recommends observing others' laughter instead of introspecting one's own, since laughter is social and 'we cannot be trusted to examine the anaesthesia of our own hearts.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For empirical work, favor observational and interactional methods (listening to group laughter, studying laughter's spread) over pure self-report introspection when researching laughter's nature and functions.
